cells.excerpt: we have no power to do good works pleasant and acceptable to God, without the grace of God by Christ preventing us, that we may have a good will
cells.shows: Grace must come first to give a good will, and then works with that will once it is given.
cells.agrees_with_coordinate: supports: grace goes before every good will (the monergist side of centre) and then 'working with us', which fits a coordinate just left of the middle
cells.binding: A historic formulary of the Church of England (Canon A 5); clergy there affirm it in the Declaration of Assent. Its standing varies by province and it is not binding across the whole Communion.

cells.section: Article XVII, Of Predestination and Election
cells.excerpt: he hath constantly decreed by his counsel secret to us, to deliver from curse and damnation those whom he hath chosen in Christ out of mankind
cells.shows: The Articles teach predestination to life as God's everlasting purpose for those chosen in Christ, and say nothing of a decree of reprobation.
cells.agrees_with_coordinate: supports the direction, and reads more monergist than 42 taken alone. No official Anglican document for the Arminian reading that many broad Anglicans hold was found, so the pull toward the centre is uncited.

cells.excerpt: not only badges or tokens of Christian men's profession, but rather they be certain sure witnesses, and effectual signs of grace, and God's good will towards us
cells.shows: The sacraments are expressly more than tokens of profession: they are effectual signs through which God works invisibly.

cells.section: Article XXVIII, Of the Lord's Supper (see also Article XXVII, Of Baptism, which retains the baptism of young children)
cells.excerpt: the Bread which we break is a partaking of the Body of Christ; and likewise the Cup of Blessing is a partaking of the Blood of Christ
cells.shows: Those who receive rightly and with faith truly partake of Christ's body and blood; the same Article rejects transubstantiation and says the body is received 'only after an heavenly and spiritual manner'.
cells.agrees_with_coordinate: supports the sacramental side; the Article's denial of transubstantiation and its stress on faith as the means of receiving make a coordinate of 5 slightly stronger than the text on its own

cells.document: Lambeth Conference 1978, Resolution 7, The Holy Spirit and the Church
cells.excerpt: recalls the entire Anglican Communion to a new openness to the power of the Holy Spirit
cells.shows: The bishops of the Communion welcomed a renewed awareness of the Spirit's power and gifts and asked that it be held within the balanced corporate and sacramental life of the parish.
cells.agrees_with_coordinate: supports: open to the gifts, with guidance and caution rather than eager seeking, which fits a moderate continuationist coordinate. The resolution names no particular gift such as tongues or prophecy; Resolution 8 of the same Conference reaffirms the ministry of healing.
cells.binding: Representative, not binding. Lambeth Conference resolutions have moral authority only and bind no province. The historic formularies are silent on this question.

cells.section: Article VII, Of the Old Testament
cells.excerpt: both in the Old and New Testament everlasting life is offered to Mankind by Christ, who is the only Mediator between God and Man
cells.shows: The Articles hold one way of salvation by Christ across both Testaments and deny that the Old Testament fathers looked only for transitory promises.
cells.agrees_with_coordinate: weaker: it supports the continuity of the two Testaments but predates dispensationalism and does not address Israel and the church, the millennium or a rapture. No Anglican formulary speaks to those questions directly.

cells.section: Article VI, Of the Sufficiency of the Holy Scriptures for Salvation (see also Article XXI: General Councils 'may err, and sometimes have erred')
cells.excerpt: whatsoever is not read therein, nor may be proved thereby, is not to be required of any man, that it should be believed as an article of the Faith
cells.shows: Nothing may be required as an article of faith that cannot be read in or proved by Scripture, and general councils are fallible.

cells.document: Canons of the Church of England
cells.date: Canons promulged 1964 and 1969, as since amended (current online edition)
cells.section: Canon A 5, Of the doctrine of the Church of England (compare Article XX: 'The Church hath power to decree Rites or Ceremonies, and authority in Controversies of Faith')
cells.excerpt: such teachings of the ancient Fathers and Councils of the Church as are agreeable to the said Scriptures
cells.shows: Church of England doctrine is grounded in Scripture and also in the Fathers and Councils so far as they agree with Scripture, giving tradition a real but subordinate place.
cells.agrees_with_coordinate: supports: this is why the coordinate sits at 65 rather than near 100. Scripture is supreme, and the Fathers, Councils and the church's own authority in controversies are kept under it.
cells.binding: Binding law for the Church of England only; other provinces have their own canons.

cells.document: Canons of the Church of England
cells.date: Canons promulged 1964 and 1969, as since amended (current online edition)
cells.section: Canon B 1, Of conformity of worship, paragraph 2
cells.excerpt: Every minister shall use only the forms of service authorized by this Canon
cells.shows: Ministers must use authorised forms of service (the Book of Common Prayer and forms approved under the Canons), with a limited discretion under Canon B 5; the Canon also covers collects, tables of lessons and the table of holy days.
cells.agrees_with_coordinate: supports. Article XXXIV lets each national church change its rites, but by common authority and not by private judgement, so the variety it allows is still liturgical.
cells.binding: Binding law for the Church of England only; other provinces authorise their own prayer books by their own canons.

notes: Axis order in compass.json is grace, table, gifts (key 'spirit'), kingdom, authority (key 'tradition'), worship; slugs are used here. Every excerpt was copied from the page or PDF actually opened on 2026-09-19 and checked as a substring of the downloaded text. The Articles text was read on the Church of England's own site, which heads it 'Convocation holden at London in the year 1562' and notes that rights in the Book of Common Prayer text are vested in the Crown (a UK matter; the 1571 text is otherwise public domain), so those excerpts are not marked link-only. The Canons (copyright the Archbishops' Council) and the Lambeth resolution (Anglican Consultative Council) are modern texts, kept under 20 words and marked link-only. The Lambeth 1978 resolution was read from the Anglican Communion Office's resolutions archive PDF; the older document-library URL (anglicancommunion.org/resources/document-library/lambeth-conference/1978/resolution-7-the-holy-spirit-and-the-church) returned 403 to automated fetches and was not read. 'Anglican (broad)' has no single binding confession across the Communion: the Articles and Canons cited are Church of England documents, used because the other provinces derive from them, and should be labelled that way on the site. Two gaps to state honestly: (1) grace, where the Articles read more monergist than the audited 42 and no official document for the Arminian reading common among broad Anglicans was found; (2) kingdom, where no formulary addresses dispensational questions and Article VII supports only the continuity of the Testaments. The 1553 Forty-two Articles condemned millenarians, but that article was dropped in 1563 and is not current, so it was not cited. The Chicago-Lambeth Quadrilateral (Lambeth 1888, Resolution 11) would be a good Communion-wide citation for authority and table but could not be opened on the Anglican Communion site in this session, so it is not quoted.
